title: Great Advocates Dont Present Options
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership distinguishes between presenting (offering facts, data, and multiple options objectively) and advocating (recommending a specific path forward based on judgment). Organizations often train leaders to present rather than advocate, optimizing for perceived objectivity at the cost of conviction. True advocacy requires proposing a specific choice and making a case for why, which exposes the advocate's real judgment. Advocates who present multiple options before staking a position weaken their case; as the saying goes, Great advocates offer up options only when their advocacy falls flat.
points: Presenting and advocating are not the same: presenting offers facts and options; advocacy demands recommending a specific path and defending it.
Organizations that train leaders to present instead of advocate create risk-averse cultures where people optimize for objectivity rather than judgment.
Advocacy while offering options is not true advocacy at all; great advocates make their case, then offer alternatives only if the initial case fails.
Conceding opposing arguments before making your case is like a trial lawyer admitting the prosecution has damning evidence before vowing to prove innocence.
Moving from information to judgment exposes real thinking; leaders who won't stake out ground without being forced to lack the conviction organizations need.
quotes: By its very definition, advocacy requires pushing for a specific outcome or choice. While presenting offers facts, data, and perspectives—often showing multiple options and their corresponding tradeoffs—advocacy demands recommending a specific path.
This is a shift from information to judgment, and it exposes advocates for what they really think and believe. Advocates don't present. They recommend.
Great advocates offer up options the moment their advocacy falls flat, and not a second before. Advocacy while offering options is not true advocacy at all.

Simply knowing when you are presenting and when you are advocating is essential. In some organizations, team members and leaders are trained to present instead of advocate.” Archived from Admired Leadership Newsletter on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
